newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's Crown Prince says peace talks must go on.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Crown Prince says peace talks must go on.

text.p: Crown Prince Hassan of Jordan urged Israel and the Palestinians on Saturday not to break peace talks after a deadly duel suicide attack in Jerusalem, saying they must make tangible progress to avoid further violence.

Describing the explosions that tore through a Jewish market on Wednesday killing 13 people and the two bombers as the latest round in a "bad nightmare" of bloodshed, the crown prince said the two sides must tackle "day-to-day lifegiving issues" to improve the status of ordinary Palestinians.
"Engagement between the core countries to the peace-making exercise is the only option," the crown prince said in an interview with Reuters.
"No progress effectively means hurting people's basic interests and investing in new generations of suicide bombers and a new wave of fanaticism."
Israel suspended talks with the Palestinian Authority after the bombing and closed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

Acting Minister of Information Nasser al-Lawzi told reporters after a cabinet meeting on Saturday which mainly focused on the crisis in peace talks that the closure could only result in more violence.
Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawnah also criticised Israel for its reaction to the bombing, saying it was critical that it perceived the Palestinian Authority as a partner and not an enemy.

Jordan, with a large Palestinian population and long borders with both Israel and the West Bank, is particularly sensitive to the potential for Palestinian unrest. It signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994 but despite continued close cooperation it has grown increasingly critical of the Jewish state.
Prince Hassan said he felt deep frustration after Wednesday's bombing in Jerusalem.
"You have warned and warned and warned against the possibility of acts of violence and loss of life. And yet somehow, like a bad nightmare, you have to live through them," he said.
Four months ago the crown prince visited the north Jordanian border territory of Baqoura after a Jordanian soldier shot dead seven Israeli girls on a school trip to the area.

"When I went to that site I made it clear that if you accept that violence is the norm then escalation would include Israeli violence on the one side and Arab violence on the other," he said. "It is our responsibility, committed to the peace process... to maintain the moderate middle ground."

The initial glow of Jordan's peace with Israel has waned since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took office last year, opposed to trading captured Arab land for peace. Popular resentment at the peace treaty is growing and King Hussein has openly doubted Netanyahu's commitment to peace.
Prince Hassan said Israel's programme of building Jewish settlements on Arab land was "dimishing the chances of any form of political breakthrough" in talks with Palestinians.
"We have made our position very clear, that settlements are null and void in legal terms," he said.

But he said practical issues like improving trade and opening Palestinian air and sea ports in Gaza should not be held to ransom by an impasse over longer-term arguments on Palestinian nationhood, refugees, borders and water rights.

"(There are) so many day-to-day lifegiving issues," Prince Hassan said. "I hope some editing can be done between the heavy, lasting and permanent issues which go way beyond the next few months and the next few years, and getting down to a full engagement for resolution of the day-to-day issues."
